title: Walter Koenig, Ensign Chekov on original Star Trek series, dead at 90
summary: Actor Walter Koenig, who played Ensign Pavel Chekov, the youthful Russian navigator on the original Star Trek television series and in several movies, has died. He was 90.

image.caption: Walter Koenig, seen here as he was honoured with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame on Sept. 10, 2012, died Monday at the age of 90, his talent agent said. (David Livingston/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Entertainment
Actor Walter Koenig, who played Ensign Pavel Chekov, the youthful Russian navigator on the original Star Trek television series and in several movies, has died. He was 90.
U.S. actor 'was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man and a loyal friend,' wrote co-star George Takei
Koenig died Monday at his home in the North Hollywood neighbourhood of Los Angeles, talent agent Zachery McGinnis said in a statement.

In Star Trek, which ran on NBC from 1966 to 1969, Chekov was the sole Communist-bloc member of the starship Enterprise's bridge staff. His friendly, supportive presence showed how the rival nations (in the far-off future in which the show was set) were capable of working together.
The TV show has also inspired multiple spinoff TV series with new casts, and conventions that draw thousands of fans.
Speaking heavily Russian-accented English, Chekov embodied fierce pride, love of poetry and great loyalty.
"My heart is heavy," Koenig's castmate George Takei said in a post on social media. "Walter was more than Chekov. He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man and a loyal friend."
George Takei as Sulu, left, and Walter Koenig as Chekov are shown in an archival photo from the set of Star Trek: The Original Series. (Getty Images)

"Walter's legacy extends far beyond the screen. Through countless convention appearances and interactions with fans, he shared his kindness, wit and appreciation with everyone fortunate enough to meet him. He understood what Star Trek meant to people and embraced the community that grew around it," McGinnis said. "Thank you, Walter, for the memories, the inspiration, and for boldly going where few have gone before."
McGinnis said Koenig died surrounded by his daughter and niece.
The baby face of the Enterprise
Series creator Gene Roddenberry said Chekov's character, who joined the show in its second season, was a response to Russian complaints about the program.

"They put in Pravda that, 'Ah, the ugly Americans are at it again. They do a space show, and they forget to include the people who were in space first,'" he said, according to The Fifty-Year Mission by Mark A. Altman and Edward Gross, an oral history of the Star Trek franchise's first 50 years.
Koenig would become the baby-faced heartthrob of the main cast.

"They wanted somebody who would appeal to eight- to 14-year-olds and the decision was to make him Russian. My fan mail came from eight- to 14-year-olds who weren't that aware of the Cold War and what was going on anyway," Roddenberry told Altman and Gross.
"At the time, the whole thing of getting fan mail was so novel to me that I read every single letter I got. I was literally getting about 700 letters a week, so that took up a lot of my spare time."
Adventure over predictability
Koenig played Chekov in seven Star Trek movies starting in 1979, as well as innumerable other spinoffs, including writing a Star Trek book, Chekov's Enterprise, in 1980.
After Star Trek ended, Koenig continued acting and wrote scripts for Family, The Incredible Hulk and other shows. He also taught part-time at UCLA and other schools.

Members of the Star Trek crew (from left): James Doohan, DeForest Kelley, Walter Koenig, William Shatner, George Takei, Leonard Nimoy and Nichelle Nichols toast the then-upcoming film Star Trek V: The Final Frontier during a news conference at Paramount Studios in Los Angeles, Calif., on Dec. 28, 1988. (Bob Galbraith/The Associated Press)
Koenig also worked in the burgeoning field of computer games, including some with a Star Trek theme. In 1995, he took a role in the CD-ROM game Maximum Surge.

"I'm at a point where I could opt in my life for complacency and a bit of predictability, or I could have one last holler — one last try for adventure," Koenig told The Associated Press in 1995. "I'm of the opinion that adventure is still a very enticing and exciting option."
He returned to the science fiction genre with occasional appearances in the syndicated 1990s TV series Babylon 5.
With files from the CBC's Jonathan Ore and John Mazerolle
